content.text: I have enough context to report. The key change: pre-diff, the cutout upload hardcoded `contentType: "image/png"`. Post-diff, it uses `form.mediaType` — a client-supplied value that server actions do NOT validate at runtime (TypeScript unions are erased). The wardrobe bucket is private, but signed URLs from Supabase serve objects with the stored `Content-Type`, so an attacker can upload arbitrary bytes and choose the served MIME type.

findings.explanation: This is a "use server" action, so `form` is deserialised from an untrusted client payload; the `mediaType: CutoutMediaType` type is only a compile-time union and is not enforced at runtime. Pre-diff the cutout upload hardcoded `contentType: "image/png"`, which meant a modified client could not influence the served MIME type. Post-diff the same client value is written verbatim into Supabase Storage as the object's stored Content-Type, and the byte payload (`form.cutoutB64`) has always been client-controlled. Because `cutoutFilename` only recognises `"image/webp"` and otherwise silently returns `"cutout.png"`, an authenticated user can send e.g. `mediaType: "text/html"` (or `"image/svg+xml"`, `"application/javascript"`) alongside an HTML/SVG payload; the object is stored under `<user>/<item>/cutout.png` with `Content-Type: text/html`. When the app later mints a signed URL via `signItemImages` and either the owner opens it directly or such a URL is embedded/shared, the browser will honour the stored MIME type and render/execute the attacker's HTML or SVG (script-bearing SVG XSS on the Supabase storage origin, MIME confusion / content spoofing generally). The Anthropic tagging call also now consumes the unvalidated `mediaType`; while Anthropic rejects unknown types, no server-side check exists to bound the value before storage writes commit. This is a control regression: replace the fixed literal with a strict allowlist rather than trusting a client-supplied string.
